figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Role of the SNR surrogate. For a set of binary parameters $\theta$, the optimal SNR $\rho_{\rm opt}$ governs detectability. Evaluating it directly for a large number of injections is computationally demanding and can become a bottleneck in population and selection-effect studies that require very large numbers of evaluations. $\Phi$asmaNet replaces this per-source computation with a neural-network surrogate that maps $\theta$ directly to $\rho_{\rm opt}$, enabling high-throughput injection campaigns in which the detectability ($\rho_{\rm opt}>8$), the sensitive volume $V\!T$, and selection effects are evaluated for large populations.
figures.headline: The surrogate maps binary parameters directly to optimal SNR, bypassing per-source waveform and inner-product computation.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Four real GWTC events reconstructed with the same waveform model and noise curve used to build the training set. Each curve is the characteristic strain $h_{c}=2f|\tilde{h}(f)|$ of the maximum-likelihood posterior sample (IMRPhenomXPHM, projected onto H1 at the event’s sky position and GPS time). The black curve is the aLIGO design noise $h_{n}=\sqrt{fS_{n}(f)}$. The events span the loudest, heaviest, and two unequal-mass systems with and without precession.
figures.headline: Four real events, spanning loud, heavy and precessing cases, rise above the aLIGO design noise curve in one detector.
citing_sentences: To illustrate the regime the surrogate operates in, Fig. 2 shows four real events from the Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalogs [4, 5], chosen to span its extremes: the loudest detection to date (GW250114 [3]), the heaviest binary (GW231123, $236\,M_{\odot}$ [2]), and two strongly unequal-mass systems that contrast a precessing configuration (GW200302, $\chi_{p}\!\approx\!0.5$ [9]) with an aligned-spin one (GW190403, $\chi_{\rm eff}\!\approx\!0.7$, $\chi_{p}\!\approx\!0.1$ [10]).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Distribution of the training labels: the phase-averaged optimal SNR $\rho_{\rm opt}$ at the reference distance $d_{L}=1000$ Mpc (shown for the $10^{5}$-sample set), on a linear scale. The label is strongly right-skewed, ranging from $\rho_{\rm opt}\lesssim 0.1$ for the lightest, least favorably oriented binaries to $\sim 10^{2}$ for the heaviest systems, with a median of $12.3$. This wide dynamic range motivates the $\log_{10}\rho_{\rm opt}$ regression target. The single-detector detection threshold $\rho_{\rm opt}=8$ is shown as a dashed line. At this reference distance $\approx 64\%$ of the samples exceed the detection threshold. The detectability of an astrophysical population follows from the $\rho_{\rm opt}\propto 1/d_{L}$ rescaling.
figures.headline: The SNR labels are strongly right-skewed, with a median of 12.3 and about 64% above the detection threshold at 1000 Mpc.
citing_sentences: The distribution of the SNR labels is shown in Fig. 3.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: $\Phi$asmaNet overview. A fixed-dimensional structured input is tokenized into a learned token set of shape $(T\times D)$ and processed by an ordered sequence of $K$ $\Phi$-Stages (each $\Phi$-Stage: standard Transformer encoder layer + $\Phi$-Refractor). The model then performs $R$ $\Phi$-Feedback passes (top-down gated feedback with forward recomputation), before token pooling (readout) and a task-specific head produce the final output.
figures.headline: The diagram shows input tokenized, refined by ordered Φ-Stages, then passed through Φ-Feedback passes before readout.
citing_sentences: As shown in Figure 4, $\Phi$asmaNet implements a staged-refinement computation pattern tailored to short, fixed-length structured inputs.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Post-calibration accuracy versus dataset size for all architectures.
figures.headline: Post-calibration accuracy grows with dataset size for ΦasmaNet and ResNet, but falls for the MLP across 100k to 1M.
citing_sentences: ResNet improves to $98.06\%$ at 1M after calibration, while the Transformer reaches $97.40\%$ and the MLP $95.64\%$ at 1M, see also Figure 5.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Before vs. after calibration performance ($100-\mathrm{MAPE}$, %) by model and dataset size. The same monotonic PCHIP calibration procedure is fitted on the validation set and applied uniformly to all models. Differences between pre- and post-calibration bars indicate how much each model benefits from this lightweight correction under the simulated setting considered here.
figures.headline: Calibration adds little for ΦasmaNet at 100k but gives a larger gain at 500k and 1M sizes.
citing_sentences: As shown in Figure 6, calibration has a dataset-size-dependent effect across models.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Training and validation loss versus epoch for $\Phi$asmaNet on the 1M dataset (seed 42, split/training seed 1337), using Huber loss in $\log_{10}\rho$ space with histogram-based weighting by_hist. The trajectories show rapid early improvement followed by a stable plateau under the shared learning-rate scheduling and early-stopping protocol.
figures.headline: Training and validation Huber loss fall quickly and then plateau, with a small gap between them.
citing_sentences: Figure 7 reports the evolution of the training and validation loss across epochs.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Within-tolerance fraction versus epoch for $\Phi$asmaNet on the 1M dataset (seed 42, split/training seed 1337). We report the fraction of samples with $\left|\rho_{\mathrm{pred}}-\rho_{\mathrm{true}}\right|/\rho_{\mathrm{true}}\leq 1\%$ in linear-SNR space on train and validation splits. This strict metric stabilizes at later epochs, consistent with convergence under the matched training protocol.
figures.headline: The fraction of samples within 1% relative error fluctuates more than the loss but stabilizes in later epochs.
citing_sentences: Figure 8 complements this view with an application-facing metric: the fraction of samples within $\pm 1\%$ relative error in linear-SNR space.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Test residual histograms for $\Phi$asmaNet on the 1M dataset (seed 42, split/training seed 1337) in linear-SNR space. Left: raw residuals ($\rho_{\mathrm{pred}}-\rho_{\mathrm{true}}$). Right: residuals after monotonic PCHIP calibration (fit on validation, applied to test).
figures.headline: Calibration concentrates test residuals more tightly around zero than the raw residuals.
citing_sentences: To directly visualize the effect of the monotonic PCHIP calibration (fit on validation, applied to test), Figure 9 compares test residual histograms in linear-SNR space before and after calibration.

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Calibrated test residuals versus true SNR for $\Phi$asmaNet on the 1M dataset (seed 42, split/training seed 1337), shown in linear-SNR space. This plot checks for SNR-dependent structure after applying the monotonic PCHIP mapping (fit on validation, applied to test).
figures.headline: Calibrated test residuals stay centered near zero across most of the true SNR range, without strong drift.
citing_sentences: Figure 10 plots calibrated test residuals versus the true SNR in linear space.

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: Predicted versus true SNR for $\Phi$asmaNet on the 1M test set (seed 42, split/training seed 1337), shown in linear-SNR space (raw predictions).
figures.headline: Before calibration, predicted SNR tracks true SNR closely across the 1M test set in linear space.
citing_sentences: Finally, Figures 11–12 provide a qualitative check via predicted-versus-true scatter plots in linear-SNR space, before and after calibration.

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: Predicted versus true SNR for $\Phi$asmaNet on the 1M test set (seed 42, split/training seed 1337), shown in linear-SNR space after monotonic PCHIP calibration (fit on validation, applied to test).
figures.headline: After calibration, predicted SNR stays close to true SNR on the 1M test set, with reduced systematic deviation.
citing_sentences: Finally, Figures 11–12 provide a qualitative check via predicted-versus-true scatter plots in linear-SNR space, before and after calibration.

abstract: Quantifying selection effects in gravitational-wave population studies requires the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of millions of simulated compact binaries, each conventionally obtained by generating a waveform and computing a noise-weighted inner product, a cost that is modest per source but becomes prohibitive in aggregate at the scale of $10^{6}$–$10^{7}$ injections. We present $\Phi$asmaNet (from Greek $\varphi\acute{\alpha}\sigma\mu\alpha$, spectrum), a compact neural architecture for structured tabular regression whose novelty is to make staged spectral representation refinement an explicit architectural prior: learned input tokens are refined by an ordered cascade of attention-based $\Phi$-Stages, each augmented by the new $\Phi$-Refractor subspace-mixing module, and then revisited through gated top-down $\Phi$-Feedback iterations. Instantiated as a surrogate mapping the $11$-dimensional parameters of precessing, higher-mode binary black hole signals (IMRPhenomXPHM) to the phase-averaged optimal SNR in a single detector at fixed Advanced LIGO design sensitivity, $\Phi$asmaNet outperforms MLP, 1D-ResNet, and Transformer-encoder baselines under a matched training protocol at every dataset scale from $10^{5}$ to $10^{6}$ samples, while using only ${\sim}\,732$k parameters. At $10^{6}$ samples it reaches $100-\mathrm{MAPE}=98.73\%$ on the held-out test set, $99.29\%$ after a rank-preserving monotonic (PCHIP) calibration, and $99.39\%$ ($R^{2}=0.9998$) in the detection-relevant regime $\rho>8$, with accuracy stable across independently generated dataset realizations. Sustaining ${\sim}\,1.2\times 10^{5}$ SNR evaluations per second on a single GPU, which processes a $10^{6}$-injection catalogue end-to-end in ${\sim}\,8.3$ s, about two orders of magnitude faster than the conventional waveform-and-inner-product calculation on a 16-core CPU, and exactly rescalable in distance through $\rho\propto 1/d_{L}$, the surrogate is fast enough for the repeated, catalogue-wide detectability evaluations that selection-effect studies demand. The fully documented pipeline is intended as a reproducible benchmark for future SNR surrogates, and out-of-the-box results on public tabular benchmarks indicate that the staged inductive bias remains competitive beyond the gravitational-wave setting. Although demonstrated here for a fixed single-detector configuration, the construction extends directly to detector networks and epoch-specific sensitivities, positioning staged neural surrogates as a practical route to keeping selection-effect estimation tractable as detector upgrades raise event rates, and with them injection-campaign demands, by orders of magnitude.

sections.body: The introduction motivates the work: selection effects in gravitational-wave population studies require signal-to-noise ratios for millions of simulated sources, and the cost of each evaluation becomes prohibitive at scale. It proposes ΦasmaNet, a neural surrogate that maps the 11 parameters of precessing, higher-mode binary black hole signals to the phase-averaged optimal SNR in one detector at fixed Advanced LIGO design sensitivity. Reported accuracy at 1M samples is 98.73 before and 99.29 after calibration, with about 8.3 s for a 10^6-injection catalogue on a single GPU. Broader cases, such as varying PSDs and detector networks, are left for future work.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Selection-effect studies need SNRs for millions of injections, and a neural surrogate could replace the per-source calculation.

sections.body: This section defines the SNR as a noise-weighted integral of the waveform over frequency and shows four real events reconstructed with the training configuration. Their single-detector SNRs in H1 range from approximately 68 for the loudest event down to approximately 9 for the most distant. The authors note that even the closed-form IMRPhenomXPHM model requires assembling and rotating many harmonic contributions on a grid of about 2×10^4 bins, and that this cost recurs at every likelihood evaluation. Interpolation tables and polynomial fits are described as inadequate once generic precessing spins are included, because the SNR no longer factorizes into a simple intrinsic and distance term. Neural networks are proposed as the alternative.
sections.heading: The Challenge of Signal-to-Noise Ratio Calculation
sections.headline: Direct SNR evaluation is costly per source, and the cost recurs at every likelihood step of a hierarchical analysis.

sections.body: Related work is grouped into three themes. Fast SNR surrogates include an MLP that maps four intrinsic parameters of aligned-spin binaries to the SNR, with speed-ups of 120 to 7.5×10^4 relative to direct waveform generation, and the gwsnr package, which uses a two-layer 32-unit perceptron on five engineered inputs with the spins compressed into one effective spin. Learned detectability models predict detection probability directly, including an emulator over a 13-dimensional space. Waveform-level surrogates interpolate the waveform itself. The authors position ΦasmaNet on the full 11-dimensional projected parameter vector, a harder regression, and say they do not claim an exhaustive benchmark against all strong tabular regressors.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior SNR surrogates use plain multilayer perceptrons on low-dimensional inputs, and the closest package reduces spins to one effective spin.

sections.body: Training labels are the phase-averaged single-detector optimal SNR computed with PyCBC for IMRPhenomXPHM signals at a reference distance of 1000 Mpc, using the H1 detector with the aLIGO zero-detuned high-power PSD. Component masses are drawn uniformly between 3 and 170 solar masses, and spin magnitudes uniformly up to 0.99. The coalescence phase is averaged over K=7 values. The regression target is log10 of the SNR plus 10^-12, and samples with SNR at or above 200 are removed before the data are split. The authors note that uniform sampling of the polar spin angle over-weights aligned configurations, and state that this is a training-coverage choice rather than an astrophysical prior.
sections.heading: Methodology
sections.headline: Labels are phase-averaged single-detector SNRs at 1000 Mpc, with 11 input features and a log10 regression target.

sections.body: Three baselines are described for comparison. The MLP has four width-256 hidden layers with GELU activations and dropout 0.1, and is trained with Huber loss. The 1D ResNet treats the 11 inputs as a length-11 sequence with a stem and four stages of two residual blocks each, ending in a 512 to 256 to 1 head. The Transformer encoder tokenizes each feature as a 128-dimensional token, applies four pre-layer-norm layers with eight heads, and mean-pools before a small regression head. Hyperparameters are not tuned per model. PCHIP calibration is applied to all architectures, which the authors state can reduce global bias without changing rank order.
sections.heading: Classic Deep Learning Architectures
sections.headline: Three baselines serve for comparison: a four-hidden-layer MLP, a 1D ResNet with 2 blocks per stage, and a Transformer encoder with four layers.

sections.body: ΦasmaNet maps the 11 standardized inputs through a linear tokenizer to T=8 tokens of dimension D=128. Three ordered Φ-Stages each apply a Transformer encoder layer with four attention heads, then a Φ-Refractor that splits the embedding into P=4 subspaces, transforms each with its own two-layer MLP, and recombines them through a softmax-gated residual. Two Φ-Feedback passes then send top-down gated updates, each followed by a full forward recomputation. A layer-norm and mean-pooling readout feeds a regression head. The full model has about 732k trainable parameters. The authors state that the local-to-global ordering across stages is a design motivation, not a verified property, and that the tokenization has not been ablated.
sections.heading: $\Phi$asmaNet: A Staged Spectral Token-Refinement Network with Recursive Feedback
sections.headline: ΦasmaNet refines eight learned tokens through three Φ-Stages and two Φ-Feedback passes, each stage adding a subspace-mixing module.

sections.body: The section argues that ΦasmaNet's contribution is how standard components are composed to impose a staged, non-homogeneous bias, not new neural primitives. It relates the Φ-Refractor to ResNeXt's split-transform-merge design, Squeeze-and-Excitation channel gating, and multi-head attention. It states that the specific combination of disjoint partitioning, subspace MLPs, and softmax-gated residual recombination has not appeared in prior work in this form, to the authors' knowledge. The spectral name is described as a metaphor. The Φ-Refractor partitions learned embedding dimensions rather than physical parameter groups, so physical specialization is left as an empirical question, and reorder or collapse ablations are deferred to future work.
sections.heading: Architectural Novelty and Design Rationale
sections.headline: Authors frame the contribution as staged inductive bias composition, with stage ordering treated as motivation rather than a verified property.

sections.body: All models share the same split, preprocessing, loss, sample weighting, AdamW optimizer with learning rate 10^-3 and weight decay 10^-4, batch size 128, up to 150 epochs, and early stopping with patience 20. ReduceLROnPlateau halves the learning rate after five epochs without validation improvement. The Huber loss uses delta 0.03 in log10 SNR space, with histogram weights clipped to 0.2 to 5.0. Accuracy is defined as 100 minus MAPE in linear SNR space on the held-out test set. The authors state that the shared settings were tuned on the MLP and not re-tuned for ΦasmaNet, and that the Φ-Refractor on and off variants differ only marginally on this task.
sections.heading: Training Protocol, Hyperparameters, and Evaluation Metrics
sections.headline: Every model shares one protocol tuned on the MLP baseline, so the ΦasmaNet comparison uses settings not chosen for it.

sections.body: Table 6 reports accuracy before and after PCHIP calibration at 100k, 500k and 1M samples for seed 42. ΦasmaNet post-calibration values are 98.37, 99.16 and 99.29. The ResNet reaches 98.06 at 1M, the Transformer 97.40 and the MLP 95.64. ΦasmaNet shows a pre-calibration dip of about 0.2 percentage points from 500k to 1M, which the authors say they do not over-interpret. Robustness checks change the training seed at 100k and regenerate the 1M dataset with seeds 43 and 44, giving post-calibration values of 99.17 and 99.29. The 100k entry uses the ON configuration although the OFF variant is marginally better there, and seed-to-seed variation is of the same order as the ablation differences.
sections.heading: Architectures Comparison Across Dataset Sizes
sections.headline: ΦasmaNet has the highest post-calibration accuracy at every size, reaching 99.29 at 1M samples versus 98.06 for ResNet.

sections.body: The training and validation Huber loss fall quickly and plateau, with a small train-validation gap. The fraction within 1% relative error fluctuates more strongly because of the histogram weighting, then stabilizes. Calibration tightens test residuals around zero and removes most global bias, without a strong SNR-dependent drift. On the 1M test set, the detection-relevant subset with true SNR above 8 is 64.0% of the test set. Calibrated accuracy on this subset is 99.39 with R^2 of 0.9998, and pre-calibration accuracy is 98.71. Inference over 10^6 samples takes about 8.3 s on one RTX 4080 with batch size 1024, against 980 s for the conventional calculation on a 16-core CPU. The model has about 732k parameters.
sections.heading: Best-model Diagnostics
sections.headline: On the SNR above 8 subset, calibrated accuracy is 99.39, and inference runs at about 1.2×10^5 evaluations per second.

sections.body: The discussion restates the 1M-sample result of 98.73 before and 99.29 after calibration, and the stability across generation seeds 43 and 44. It supports ΦasmaNet as a compact surrogate for simulation-driven selection-effect work, while stating the limits: one detector (LIGO-Hanford), a fixed representative PSD and waveform approximant, an 11-dimensional parameter input rather than strain, and a bounded range of SNR below 200. Transfer to other PSDs, observing epochs, or detector networks is not established. A direct comparison with earlier neural SNR surrogates is not possible because their setups differ. Planned extensions include detector networks by quadrature sum, a noise-averaged detection probability, broader ablations, and gradient-boosted tree baselines.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: The authors support ΦasmaNet for simulation-driven selection-effect studies and list its single-detector, fixed-PSD limits.

sections.body: The training code is publicly released for ΦasmaNet with and without the Φ-Refractor, and for the MLP, ResNet and Transformer baselines. The section gives the repository as the PhasmaNet-SNR project under the giannis00 account on GitHub. The discussion describes this release as a reproducible benchmark against which future SNR surrogates can be compared. The section does not describe the data files or a license.
sections.heading: Code Availability
sections.headline: Training code for ΦasmaNet and its three baselines is publicly released on GitHub.

sections.body: The appendix tests whether the staged inductive bias transfers to public tabular benchmarks, using the SNR-task configuration unchanged and no dataset-specific tuning. On YearPredictionMSD, ΦasmaNet reaches an RMSE of 8.8738, placing rank 6/10, within 0.09 of the best reference, NODE at 8.784. On Covertype it reaches accuracy 0.9664, placing rank 2/9, behind only FT-Transformer at 0.970. On Epsilon, a 2000-feature input outside the tokenizer's design range, accuracy is 0.8915 and ROC-AUC 0.9950, near the bottom of the ranking. The authors call Epsilon a stress test rather than a like-for-like comparison, and note that the reference architectures were tuned per dataset with Bayesian optimization.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix lists out-of-the-box results on YearPredictionMSD, Covertype and Epsilon, with no dataset-specific tuning.
